idiom_name: frozen dataclass nodes + tuple path; dataclasses.replace rebuilds the parent
implementation_notes: There is no zipper in the standard library, but the structure is short: frozen dataclasses (or NamedTuples) for the tree, a frozen Loc pairing the focus with a tuple of (parent, index) frames, and dataclasses.replace(parent, kids=...) to rebuild the parent on the way up. Tuples are the real immutability primitive - frozen is shallow, so children must be tuples, frozensets or other frozen values, never lists - and replace() re-runs __init__/__post_init__, so validation placed there executes once per step up the path. For XML-like documents the standard library takes the other route (xml.etree.ElementTree, and lxml with real parent links), and a whole-tree rewrite is more simply a recursive function with replace.
pitfalls: frozen=True is shallow: a list or dict field is still mutated through any reference and makes the instance unhashable - use tuple/frozenset for children so sharing stays safe.
dataclasses.replace() re-runs the constructor (and __post_init__) on every rebuild, so invariants, caches or logging placed there run once per level of the path.
Python's recursion limit (about a thousand frames) caps recursive navigation; carry the explicit path and iterate when trees can be deep.
Mutable default arguments and shared module-level nodes are aliased into every version; build each level from fresh tuples.
